reading.heading: The 5 Ws and H
reading.explanation:
Every news story answers six questions: **Who? What? Where? When? Why? and How?** Reporters use them as a checklist before writing and again before publishing. If one answer is missing, the reader will notice the gap, so go back and ask.

Not every answer carries equal weight. In a fire, what happened and whether anyone was hurt matter most; in an election, who won. The most important answers belong in the first sentence.

Why and how often take longer to find and may come later in the story, or in a follow-up. If an answer is not yet known, say so clearly rather than guessing.

The ceremony took place at the City Museum in Leeds.

reading.heading: Open and closed questions
reading.explanation:
A **closed question** can be answered in a word or two, often yes or no: "Was the school closed today?" "How many people were injured?" Closed questions are good for checking facts and pinning down details.

An **open question** starts with what, how, why or tell me about, and invites a longer answer: "What happened when the alarm went off?" Open questions get stories, feelings and details you would never think to ask about.

A good interview usually starts open, to let the person talk, and then uses closed questions to confirm names, numbers and times.

reading.heading: Follow-up questions
reading.explanation:
A **follow-up question** builds on what the person has just said. It shows you are listening, and it often produces the best details.

Useful follow-ups include:
- "Can you give me an example?",
- "What happened next?",
- "Why was that important to you?"
- "How did you feel at that moment?"

Listen for vague words — a lot, soon, many, problems — and ask for specifics: "How many is a lot?"

Do not move to your next prepared question if the answer opened a better one. Your list of questions is a guide, not a script.

reading.heading: Quoting and attributing
reading.explanation:
A **direct quote** uses a person’s exact words inside quotation marks. **Attribution** tells the reader who said them: "We will reopen on Monday," said Maria López, the school’s head teacher.

Use said most of the time; it is neutral. Words like claimed, admitted or insisted suggest doubt or guilt, so use them only when they are accurate. Never change the words inside quotation marks.

If you rephrase the idea in your own words, it is a **paraphrase** and takes no quotation marks, but it still needs attribution: López said the school would reopen on Monday. Give a person’s full name and role the first time, and usually the surname after that.

reading.heading: The inverted pyramid
reading.explanation:
Most news stories follow the **inverted pyramid**: the most important facts come first, followed by supporting details, background and less important information. The shape is an upside-down triangle — wide at the top with the key facts, narrow at the bottom.

This structure serves readers who stop early: even after one paragraph, they know the news. It also helps editors, who can cut from the bottom without losing the core of the story.

After the lede, add the next most important facts, then quotes, then context and background.

examples.answer: Floods closed 12 schools in the northern district on Tuesday.
About 3,000 students were sent home. Officials expect schools to reopen on Thursday.
The district last flooded in 2019, when the river rose two metres.
examples.explanation: Background that can be cut if needed.

reading.heading: Headlines and ledes
reading.explanation:
A **headline** is a short title that tells the main news and makes people want to read. News headlines use short, strong words, the present tense for past events, and often drop small words like the and a: "Storm closes city schools".

The **lede** is the first sentence of the story. A news lede gives the most important facts — usually who, what, when and where — clearly, in about 25–35 words. Write the lede first; if you cannot, you may not yet know what the story is.

The headline and lede must agree; a headline should never promise more than the story shows.

examples.answer: Council approves new cycle lanes
The city council voted on Wednesday to build 20 kilometres of cycle lanes by 2027.
examples.explanation: Who, what, when in one sentence.

examples.answer: Cars banned from city centre!
examples.explanation: Not true if only lanes are planned.

reading.heading: Fact, opinion and doubt
reading.explanation:
Reporters separate what is known from what someone thinks. A **fact** can be checked: a date, a vote count, a quote from a document. An **opinion** is a view or judgement: "The new law is unfair." In a news story, opinions belong to named sources, not to the reporter.

When facts are not certain, choose careful words:
- according to
- police said
- may have
- is believed to
- has not been confirmed.

Never present a guess as a fact. "The fire was caused by a cigarette" needs proof; "Fire officials said the fire may have started from a cigarette" reports what is known.

"This decision is a mistake," said opposition leader Rui Costa.
examples.explanation: The opinion belongs to the source.

reading.heading: Summarising a source fairly
reading.explanation:
Journalists often summarise reports, speeches and studies. A **fair summary** keeps the original meaning while using fewer words of your own.

- Pick out the main points and the most important evidence.
- Do not add your opinion, and do not leave out facts that would change how readers understand it — such as a limitation the authors mention.
- Keep qualifiers: if a study says a drug "may reduce" symptoms, do not write that it "cures" them.
- Name the source clearly: "The report, published by the Health Ministry on Tuesday, says…".

Walking cures high blood pressure, scientists say.
The authors said the results need to be tested in older people.

reading.heading: Checking facts with two sources
reading.explanation:
A claim is much stronger when **two independent sources** support it. Independent means they did not get the information from each other or from the same original source.

Always ask how a source knows: did they see it themselves, read it in a document, or hear it from someone else? First-hand information is stronger than second-hand.

Tell readers how you know: "according to the police report", "said two witnesses who saw the crash". If you cannot confirm a detail, leave it out or clearly label it as unconfirmed. Being second with the right story is better than being first with the wrong one.

reading.heading: On the record and off the record
reading.explanation:
Tell sources how you will use what they say, and agree on the rule before the information is shared, not after.

- **On the record** means you can publish what they say and use their name.
- **On background** means you can use the information but must not name the person; you might describe them ("a senior official").
- **Off the record** means you cannot publish the information at all; it may only guide your reporting.

Named sources are best because readers can judge who is speaking. Use anonymous sources only when there is real risk to the person and a strong public interest, and explain why they are not named.

reading.heading: Reporting numbers with context
reading.explanation:
A number alone says little. Add a **comparison, a base and a source**. "Robberies fell from 40 to 30" becomes much clearer with "in a city of 200,000" and with the trend over the last five years.

Give a percentage only when the base is clear: a fall from 40 to 30 is 25%. Round when precision does not matter: "about 200,000", "nearly a third".

Never report a small change as a big trend, and be careful with records and firsts. Always say where the numbers come from and over what period.

reading.heading: Being fair and balanced
reading.explanation:
**Fair stories** give the people involved a chance to respond. If you report a criticism of a person or organisation, contact them before publishing and include their answer, or say they did not respond.

Use neutral verbs and words: said is fairer than claimed; avoid loaded words such as disaster, scandal or miracle unless a named source uses them.

Balance does not mean treating two unequal positions as equal. If the evidence strongly supports one side, say so; giving equal space to a fringe view can mislead readers.

reading.heading: News ledes and feature ledes
reading.explanation:
A **news lede**, also called a straight or hard lede, gives the main facts in one or two sentences: who, what, when and where. It suits urgent news.

A **feature lede** may start with a person, a scene or a surprising detail to draw the reader in. It must then reach the point quickly in a **"nut paragraph"** that says why the story matters now.

Choose the lede that fits the story: a factory fire needs a direct lede; a story about one family’s recovery from the fire can begin with a moment. Avoid opening with a question, a dictionary definition or the weather unless it truly matters.

reading.heading: Quoting and paraphrasing well
reading.explanation:
Use a **direct quote** when the words are vivid, emotional or important because of who said them. Use a **paraphrase** when the idea matters but the wording is dull or long.

Never change the words inside quotation marks. A **partial quote** is allowed if it does not change the meaning: The mayor called the plan "a long-overdue fix".

Place the attribution after the first sentence of a longer quote: "We need new equipment," Ortiz said. "The old playground is unsafe." Check every quote against your notes or recording before publishing.

News sentences are **short, active and specific**.

reading.heading: Following the documents
reading.explanation:
Strong stories often rest on **documents**:
- budgets
- contracts
- court files
- inspection reports
- company accounts.

Many are public records that you can request. Read the original, not someone’s summary. Note dates, names, amounts and signatures, and build a timeline. Ask what a document does not say: a missing year, a blank signature, a contract with no tender.

When you request records, be specific and polite: the exact title, the date range and the office that holds them. Keep copies and note how and when you obtained each one.

reading.heading: Reading data with suspicion
reading.explanation:
Numbers can mislead even when they are accurate.

- Adjust for size: spending that rises while the population grows may be falling per person.
- Know the difference between a **mean** (average) and a **median** (middle value): a few very high incomes pull the mean up, so the median often describes a typical person better.
- Ask how a survey chose its respondents: an online poll where anyone can vote shows only those who chose to answer.
- Report the **margin of error** for polls.
- Compare like with like, and ask for the full dataset when you can, not just the chart.

reading.heading: Verifying images and online claims
reading.explanation:
Viral images and posts can be old, edited or from somewhere else entirely.

- Check **provenance**: who first posted it, and when?
- Run a **reverse image search** to find earlier copies.
- Look for details you can confirm: street signs, shop names, weather, shadows, landmarks, language on posters.
- Contact the person who posted it and ask how they got it.
- Look for the same event in independent reports.

If you cannot confirm it, label it clearly as unverified or leave it out. Speed is never a good reason to publish an unverified claim.

examples.answer: The “flood today” photo first appeared online in 2017.
The road signs in the video are in Portuguese, not Spanish.

reading.heading: Asking accountability questions
reading.explanation:
When a powerful person avoids a question, **ask it again, precisely**. Keep questions short, and use closed questions when you need a specific fact: "Was a public tender held — yes or no?" Do not accept a general statement as an answer; note it and return to your question.

Use **silence**: after a short or evasive answer, wait. People often fill the silence with more information.

In your story, quote both the exact question and the exact non-answer, so readers can judge. Stay courteous and firm; the goal is the answer, not a confrontation.

reading.heading: Structuring a long feature
reading.explanation:
A long feature needs a clear design. Open with a scene or a person, then state the stakes in a **nut paragraph**: what is happening, why it matters now.

Then move through sections:
- background
- conflict
- evidence
- what happens next.

**Braid** the human story with the explanation, returning to the main person between sections so readers stay connected. Use subheadings or clear changes of scene.

End with an image, moment or quote that echoes the opening, not with a summary. Cut anything that does not serve the central question.

reading.heading: Explaining complexity clearly
reading.explanation:
Complex topics lose readers when the writer assumes knowledge.

- **Define each technical term** the first time you use it, in plain words.

- Use one precise analogy, and check that it does not mislead.
- Use concrete examples and numbers people can picture: "enough water to fill 40 Olympic pools".

reading.heading: Ethics: harm, privacy and conflicts
reading.explanation:
Journalists balance the public’s right to know against the harm a story may cause.

- Ask: is there a real **public interest**, or only curiosity?
- Could the story identify someone who should be protected, such as a child or a victim of crime?
- Have sources understood how their words will be used?

Declare **conflicts of interest**: if you own shares in a company you cover, or a relative works there, tell your editor and step aside. Do not pay sources for information. The aim is to minimise harm without hiding the truth.

examples.answer: The mayor’s use of public money is news; her children’s school grades are not.
A 15-year-old witness, who cannot be named, said…
I can’t cover this company — my brother is on its board.

reading.heading: Truth, opinion and fair comment
reading.explanation:
Accuracy protects readers and writers. A true, well-sourced **statement of fact** is the strongest position a journalist can take. **Opinion** is different: label it clearly as opinion and base it on facts you state.

Be especially careful with **serious allegations**: have documents or at least two reliable sources, give the person a chance to respond, and report their reply. When you report what an official or a court said, attribute it precisely.

Make corrections promptly and visibly. Laws differ between countries; this is not legal advice, so follow your editor’s guidance.

archivedLessons.title: Be fair and balanced
archivedLessons.tip: Fair stories give the people involved a chance to respond. If you report a criticism, ask the person criticized for their side before you publish. archivedLessons.title: Ethics: harm, privacy and conflicts
archivedLessons.tip: Journalists balance the public’s right to know against possible harm. Ask: Is there a public interest, not just curiosity? Can a person be identified who should not be, such as a minor or a victim? Have you told sources how their words will be used? Disclose conflicts of interest: if you own shares in a company you cover, say so or step aside. Do not pay sources. Minimize harm without hiding the truth.

archivedLessons.title: Truth, opinion and fair comment
archivedLessons.tip: Accuracy protects readers and the writer. A statement of fact that is true and well sourced is the strongest position. Opinion is different: label it clearly and base it on stated facts. Be careful with serious allegations: have documents or two reliable sources, offer the person a chance to respond, and report their reply. When you report a statement from an official source or court, attribute it precisely. Corrections should be prominent and prompt. This is not legal advice; follow your editor’s guidance.
